speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAM RESPECTING TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of hon. Members a proposal which was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and which will be submitted to the House for approval in the Supplementary Estimates of the Department of Industry. It is a program for the advancement of industrial technology, which is designed to promote the growth of Canadian industry by the application of scientific and technological advances to the development of new products and processes of benefit to the national economy.
The basic concept of the program is to help industry help itself to improve its technological capability and to expand its innovation activity by underwriting development projects which involve a genuine technical advance and which, if successful, offer good prospects for commercial exploitation. Assistance under the program will be available to individual firms or groups of firms which have the capabilities and facilities to undertake the development work, and to manufacture and market the results.
Support will be concentrated on the development of producer goods and manufacturing processes, which serve to increase productivity and contribute directly to economic growth. Wherever possible, advantage will be taken of Canada's natural resources, skills and environment to establish a unique capability or technical leadership. Preference will be given to projects which offer maximum return to the economy and the broadest distribution of benefits to the nation as a whole.
The initiative for proposing development projects and responsibility for their direction and execution will rest with industry. Costs will be shared by the Government and the industrial firm, and in the event the project is successful and the results are brought into commercial usage, the firm will be required to repay the Government's contribution. In order to ensure expeditious and effective exploitation of the results of the development projects, title to patents, designs, information and equipment resulting from the project will vest in and remain the property of industrial firms. However, firms will be expected to exploit the results of the project in Canada.
It is hoped this program will improve the position of Canadian industry in relation to its foreign competitors who enjoy the advantage of substantial government financial support for their research and development endeavours. It is also expected that it will help to create an industrial environment attractive to our best qualified scientific, technical, and managerial personnel. The program is envisaged as a catalyst for technical progress, and since investment in research and development is economically regenerative, the potential return to the economy could be many times the original outlay.
It is estimated that expenditures in the fiscal year 1965-66 to initiate this program will be $5 million, which amount will be included in the Supplementary Estimates of the Department of Industry and placed before the House for approval. For future years it is expected that the rate of expenditure will build up progressively, depending upon industry's needs and ability to expand its level of technical activity.

subsubtopic: USE OF CHLORPROMAZINE IN TREATMENT OF PSYCHIATRIC PATIENTS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by virtue of Standing Order 26 I would ask leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. Last November in a meeting of the Special Committee on Food and Drugs I made mention of the concern of my fellow medical practitioners about the long term effects of some of the potent drugs we are now using in the treatment of psychiatric patients. I referred then to a paper delivered to the Canadian Psychiatric Association making observations about skin pigmentation problems following long-term treatment on high dosages of the medication known generically as chlorpromazine. I referred also to a report in the Journal of the Canadian Medical Association on liver damage, and deaths resulting from the use of this drug.
Use of Chlorpromazine
At that time I asked the witness drug manufacturer, who was not the original developer of the drug, about his studies and clinical testing of his product. He stated that he had none; that he was not making, nor did he seem to intend to have made, any clinical studies on the ground that this was only the responsibility of the original developer. I also discovered that this manufacturer had no staff physician to whom physicians could immediately refer if they encountered some unexpected side effect in the use of this potent drug.
Medical integrity insists that the best interest of the patient is served by treating him with medicines compounded under the most scrupulous conditions, that have been clinically proven for efficacy as to purity, solubility and stability of the active chemical and the dosage form offered to the patient, whose supplier's processes are under continuous medical supervision, and who have a staff physician available continuously for consultation by the patient's physician in the event of unexpected reactions.
It was my intention to wait until the deliberations of the Committee of this House offered an appropriate moment to accent this problem and concern. But in a recent issue of the Canada Gazette, part I of May 8, I observed a notice that a chemical company was applying to the Commissioner of Patents for the right to a manufacturing patent developed by another pharmaceutical house. As I understand it, there is no legal block to the Commissioner ordering this. As it is not regarded as a new drug, the Federal Government requires no clinical tests, no studies, no reporting of any nature of the dosage form to be presented, simply the right to compound the chemical.
Yet this is even more potent a drug than the one with which the scientists were concerned at the Canadian Psychiatric Association. Trifluoperazine, as I discovered the application to concern, is the most potent of all the potent phenothiazines. The tablet form of it never contains more than 10 milligrams of the active ingredient. The present manufacturer's literature states that:
At the dosage levels used in mental hospitals, neuromuscular reactions are seen in a significant number of patients. These side effects are manifested not only as a transient stimulation or jitteriness, but also as dystonias, or pseudo-Parkinsonism.
Obviously it must not only be administered with great care, but the physician and patient must know that it is manufactured under the

June 4, 1965
Use of Chlorpromazine conditions and to the standards upon which medical integrity insists.
I submit therefore that this is more-much more-than a simple patent matter to be settled by even good technicians. I hold no brief for the owners of the patent per se. But I do hold a brief for the protection and welfare of the Canadian people. So I urge the Minister to bring this immediate matter into the purview of her Department and also all future applications for the licensing of potent medicines made under patent; or I urge that all arrangements between the owner of the patent to make potent medicines and other drug manufacturers shall be conditional upon:
(a)	Being in possession of a certificate indicating that the proposed new producer complies with the manufacturing standards of the Food and Drug Directorate of Canada;
(b)	That the new producer is in possession, and prepared to submit evidence to the Food and Drug Directorate of Canada, of studies of a controlled laboratory of a clinical nature demonstrating safety and availability or efficacy of the dosage form offered;
(c)	That the dosage form employed in the aforementioned studies shall have been manufactured by the same method and process as that proposed to be sold by the applicant;
(d)	That the processes of the proposed new product are under the medical supervision of a physician licensed to practice in Canada and that a physician on the full time permanent staff of the applicant is available for consultation at any hour by any physician in practice in Canada or by the Food and Drug Directorate.
I, and other physicians in medical practice, realize that the drugs we have have proven efficacious when made under the supervision of the medical profession. Yet they can be a two-edged sword. So for the sake of the people of Canada I ask the Minister to act now, under an emergency order if necessary, and set strict standards before we encounter a situation that should-and could-have been prevented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in connection with the announcement made last night by the Prime Minister regarding uranium, there are one or two matters that were far from clear. The first is, in view of the existence of contacts with the United States and the United Kingdom for uranium and the revision of the terms of those contracts to assure what the Minister referred to as verification, have consultations taken place with the representatives of those two nations and have they agreed to that amendment of the existing contracts? Second, what is the meaning of "verification"? Does that mean inspection or is this word used in order to allow the Republic of France to make purchases of uranium by simply making a declaration that the uranium is going to be used for civil purposes? What is the meaning of "verification"?
It is obvious that the Prime Minister steered away from the word that has always been used in the past "inspection", namely the right to inspect within the country receiving the uranium, its facilities to ensure that the use of the uranium supplied shall be for domestic purposes?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SALE TO FRANCE-APPROACH TO U.S. AND U.K. GOVERNMENT RESPECTING INSPECTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as far as the first part of the question is concerned there have been consultations, before this policy was adopted, with the United Kingdom and United States Governments because of our previous association with them in regard to uranium policy matters. The Governments concerned understand and appreciate the policy we have announced. This policy, in the announcement, was stated to refer to contracts that will be made, and it is not the intention of this Government unilaterally to interfere with the two existing contracts. We have one with the United States which will be completed, I believe, by the end of this year and one with the United Kingdom on which over half of the uranium has been delivered.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, June 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Mac-Naught:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;

That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders;
1.	(a) That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 30 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of main estimates; interim supply; and supplementary or additional estimates excepting supplementary or additional estimates introduced after the main estimates have been approved, and excepting always the final supplementary or additional estimates;
(b)	That the number of supply motions be reduced from six to four; and
(c)	That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-four members to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these orders, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the Committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in. such sitting, interrupt the proceedings and forthwith
June 4, 1965

put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(7)	No motion made by a Minister under Sections (5) and (6) of this Standing Order shall provide for the allocation of a period of time shorter than two days for the second reading, two days for the committee stage, and one day for the third reading of any bill. For the purposes of this section, third reading shall be deemed to have been considered for one day provided the order for third reading is called as the first item under Government Orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, if necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that day, unless it is disposed of earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
(8)	During debate on any item of business or stage thereof for which an allocation of time has been made under this Standing Order, if an amendment is proposed which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker materially changes the item of business or stage thereof and which raises any issue for whcih in the opinion of Mr. Speaker, there has not been or otherwise will not be an adequate opportunity for discussion, Mr. Speaker may announce an extension of not more than two days to the allocated period of time.
3.	That the orders of this House under numbered paragraph 1, the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these Orders, and the new Standing Order 15A be continued in effect until the end of the next ensuing session, unless this House otherwise orders.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I move an amendment I wish to make some general comments on this subject. I agree with Members who have paid tribute to the Speakers we had in the House of Commons. Although I do not intend to deal with the subject of the Speakership at this time I am in hearty accord with those who have praised the calibre of the men who have occupied the Chair.
I am one who has always defended Mr. Beaudoin, the Speaker when I first became a member of Parliament. I think he was the victim of certain wild despots who happened to be governing the country at that time. He had one especially good quality. He taught the new Members the virtue of relevancy and warned them against repetition. I think that is a good start for all Members; it is good for them to keep those important points in mind.
I wish also to pay tribute to the committee on the rules which worked so hard on the recommendations we now have before us. It might be said that the Members of this committee were less senior and less experienced than those who have sat on other committees on procedure, but this might have had a good effect inasmuch as they were probably more ready to recommend measures of reform. At the same time I make no apology for criti-

cizing certain of the recommendations which have been brought forward. I feel that, at the risk of being accused of being ultra-Conservative, I can within my party principles make points which in the final analysis will be helpful to a number of these recommendations.
Speaking of the criticism of Parliament which has been made both outside and inside this House, some Members have said that if we cannot stand criticism we should not be here. I agree with this point of view to a certain extent but I deplore the fact that many Members continually harp on unfortunate incidents here and deride Parliament when they themselves are as much to blame as anybody. I recall reading in a newspaper a short while ago that a Member of Parliament had delivered an address in Montreal telling his audience what was wrong with Parliament. He delivered his address on a certain day of the week when, here in Ottawa, we were discussing a most important measure. Another example of what I have in mind is contained in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of May 20. It is just an example. Very commendably, this newspaper is publishing reports of statements by Members of all parties. In this particular instance the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) dealt with changes in procedure in the House of Commons. Far from being worried about closure and the other proposals which might stifle debate, he said:
The exasperation of the public has a solid justification. Parliament in carrying out the various purposes for which it exists functions inefficiently.
The hon. Member added:
The weakness of the Government proposals is that they do not go far enough, a (2:40 p.m.)
Then the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) who, like the hon. Member for Greenwood, has not been here too long but has somehow become very much of an authority on the rules, takes a position exactly opposite, I am sure, to the one most members of his party would take. He talks about how good everything is now in Parliament. He says:
Those commentators who sit back and take a calm second look at public affairs are saying that in spite of the noise of the fray which disturbed those who watched the battle from day to day in the rail seats, the legislative accomplishment of the Government in the short span of two years has been considerable.
I am not quarrelling with these remarks, Mr. Speaker, but I would like Members to stand up and say that they are proud of Parliament instead of deriding Parliament in the press all the time because we here in
June 4, 1965

this chamber are the ones who are responsible for Parliament. Everybody has their own ideas about what is wrong with Parliament. I think it is quite simple. I think there is too much talk and there is not enough maturity and self-discipline in this place.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Sit down, then.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Come out from behind the curtain and say that.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
We are following the British system. We have not the necessary ingredients of maturity and self-discipline, and we have superimposed on us some of the weaknesses of the American system in the form of lobbying and reading speeches. Mr. Speaker, I now want to deal with the role of the Opposition. Many have said that the duties of the Opposition are easy to define. I have been here a considerable time. I checked before coming into the chamber and found that in fact I have spent more time in Opposition than I have in government, and I do not think too many Members of the Government can say they have been in Opposition more than they have been in government. This shows that there are two different points of view in this argument. I recall the stories in 1962 toward the end of the previous Government. They were that the trouble with Parliament was that the Government could not organize the business properly. Then the Government was changed and now it is the Opposition that is to blame; they are opposing everything. I have always been more proud of the fact that I have been a Member of the Opposition than even of being a Member on the Government side, if that distinction has to be made.
I remember that when I came here it was at the time the Russians were first visiting Canada. A former Minister of Fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, who was, incidentally, in my opinion a very good Minister, very kindly included me in the visit to parts of New Brunswick with the Minister of Fisheries from Russia. I wondered for a time why he was giving me this attention, a poor little Member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. When I was introduced to the Russian minister I realized what was behind it. I was introduced as fisheries critic and a Member of the Opposition and of course the Russian minister immediately said, "I have never heard of the Opposition".
This Parliament may have its troubles. I recall reading in the paper the other day that someone had done an anthropological
House of Commons Procedures study of the Indians in Canada, and after a great deal of research it was found, as most of us know, that the Indian is competent, mentally alert and capable of anything. In this story it was suggested that perhaps some day an Indian could become Prime Minister of the country. Someone else, knowing Indians have a very desirable trait of not talking unless they really have something to say, added that it might be a good idea if we had a House of Commons full of Indians.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: We have it now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Yes, instead of all chiefs.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to bring to the attention of the House some of my thinking with regard to the role of the Opposition. I intend to point out six dangers there may be in time limited debates and to state my own position on the matter of time limitation or the guillotine or closure as it has been called. We have the traditional statements from the authorities. Jennings said:
The Opposition demands that policies be formulated openly, and the consequences of policies revealed. Parliament compels the Government to defend itself by open and rational argument;-
He also adds, which is important:
-but it also compels the Opposition to state what is the alternative.
Gladstone said:
Your business is not to govern the country. It is, if you think fit, to call to account those who do govern it.
Although I could not find the reference, I think it was Disraeli who said that the Opposition's duty is essentially to oppose. I do not agree with the statement another person made, nor do I suggest it is in the same category as these authorities I have quoted, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when in Opposition at the end of the twenty-fifth Parliament said that the Government should be defeated at any cost by any means. This, of course, was one of the manifestations of the boys in Opposition in those days. I think most of our problems here now can be laid at their doorstep and I said this in Windsor, the home city of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, not very long ago.
Parliamentary debate is not just for the presentation of the public views of each Member's constituency. These ideas must be brought together by some meeting of minds, by some national consensus. Even with rigid party discipline, which we would all hope was not as strict as it is, it behooves a good Government to pay attention to those grass
June 4, 1965

House of Commons Procedures roots opinions and then to take the stand on particular legislation that they deem best for the nation. So if an autocratic government such as that in 1956 decides on legislation that is questionable, the only weapon the Opposition has is to talk and expose the issue to the public. That is why I think there is a great deal of wisdom in the thought that was put forward by the hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) of a week's delay in order to allow the issue to be made known across the country, to be considered by the people in the ridings and to give us time to receive their opinions.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Part of our responsibility as Members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is to prevent any form of tyranny or oppression. This is one of our main functions if we are to preserve the institution of Parliament and all its freedoms. Since coming to this chamber I have heard there are three freedoms in Parliament, freedom to speak, freedom of assembly and freedom of organization. I have often wondered where these three freedoms came from and, although I did not find the original source, to a certain extent I found them credited to the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), and this gives me an opportunity to pay tribute to the work that he has done here for many years. May I also refer hon. Members to a recent address he gave to the Chamber of Commerce in Winnipeg, which I think is a must for everyone interested in the rules regardless of whether they consider themselves great reformers or are people like myself who feel there is still some good in the rules which we now have.
For these privileges, these freedoms I have mentioned to be effective, there must be in existence a set of rules which among other things gives the fullest opportunity to expose not only the weakness of any legislation that may be brought forward but, just as important, an opportunity to expose any highhanded illusions that a particular Government may have developed, whatever the reason.
In our British parliamentary system the checks on the misuse of power are concealed in the rules and are not defined in particular ways. They are certainly not as apparent as in written constitutions such as in the United States. However, the fact that these rules, these restraints on the misuse of power, have been developed through their use in our procedure, causes me to guard them more jealously. Should we forget any of these parliamentary freedoms for any reason, then our
[Mr. Bell.)
loss and damage are greater than that suffered by those bodies which follow the written constitution system.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the proposals before us have two separate divisions. There are the proposals which have particular reference to time limits on debate and the other individual measures. Then there will also be brought forward for discussion in Committee the latter proposals, such as removal of appeals from rulings of the Speaker and the reduction of the question period to half an hour. I am confining my remarks to the first part of these proposals having to do with closure and the like and I will save my criticism of some of the others until such time as we get into Committee.
I think there are six inherent dangers involved in any sort of time limit on debate. First, I think it would be silly, merely to get things done, to bring into Parliament reform measures which limit our freedom of speech. I recall last year, when the student loans legislation was brought forward, that we were all aware as Members of Parliament that this legislation had to be passed before the beginning of the September university term. Everyone buckled down and got into a good mood. We made some amendments and the legislation went forward without too much trouble and in good form. If we want to do the job we can. I do not think, just because we took time off last summer, rightly or wrongly, to debate a very important matter for some people, the question of a new flag which scrapped our old traditions, that we should have this put forward as the main justification for rule changes.
Second, I do not think that merely because a rule is not working we should scrap it. In his introductory speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) referred to appeals from the Speaker's rulings and said that they were being used for political purposes, thus leaving the implication that they should be abolished. I admit that to some extent they have been used for political purposes but I do not think they have been used in any overall, strategic way except at the time of the pipe line debate when closure was used. Therefore, such a reason as this would to me seem highly dangerous.
Third, as everyone knows, any decrease in our legislative power means an alternative increase in the power of the executive or the Civil Service. I am highly suspicious, Mr. Speaker, of such a move knowing that the Government is run by many former civil

servants. I do not say this is intentional, but I do want to go on record as saying that I am highly suspicious of civil servants such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), and I could also include the Prime Minister, who have spent many years in the Civil Service and who want to reduce the important legislative branch of our system of Government.
Another danger to me, Mr. Speaker, is that any reduction in time, which would undoubtedly affect the backbenchers first, would mean that there would be a corresponding reduction in the matter of local constituency references in Parliament. The question period is an opportunity for backbenchers and others to bring matters of urgent national importance from their local regions to the attention of Parliament and hope for action as a result. I for one feel that any reduction of or time limit on the question period will greatly reduce the effectiveness of the backbencher and his ability to bring matters forward which are of a local nature.
Another danger, which is probably as important as any of them, is this. I object to changes in our procedures merely to deal with a particular situation. We have in this House a minority Government situation and many of our problems result from this fact. To begin with, it would be incorrect to assume that we should implement permanent legislation because of this situation. If we had an occasion when the country was at war, I would think that many members would be willing to accelerate business expediently as is necessary at such time. But I would hate to see rules brought in in a time of war on a permanent basis which might determine future action. In view of those dangers, Mr. Speaker, I find that I must take a firm and hard position against any time limit on debate. I am opposed to any restriction whatsoever on the freedoms I have mentioned, particularly the freedom of speech.

House of Commons Procedures opportunity to speak as a private Member on either a local or national matter is denied, dire consequences may result and the rules themselves will be twisted in a clandestine way to prevent Members from being heard. I am not referring to time wasting by appealing Speaker's rulings or by phony questions of privilege and the like but rather the basic opportunities for private Members to express their opinions. If these are denied the ultimate result will be a tragic breakdown of Parliament and perhaps our democratic way of life will be placed in jeopardy.
Surely the election of 1957, when those rascals responsible for the pipe line debate were unceremoniously kicked out of office, is still in our minds and is a sufficient lesson for those who sit across the aisle from me. Questions arising in the House of Commons shall be decided by a majority of voices other than that of the Speaker, and when the Voices are equal, but not otherwise, the Speaker shall have a vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few days we have had what I consider to be perhaps one of the most interesting debates, certainly one of the most thoughtful and serious debates I have ever heard in the 12 or 13 years I have had the privilege of sitting in this House. This particular debate concerning alteration of the rules under which this Parliament operates is perhaps one of the most serious debates that we could possibly entertain here. The reason is that the result of this debate will place the road and place the boundaries of the road for future pieces of legislation and discussions in this House.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a great many of the persons who are so anxious to streamline the rules are very sincere in their desire to do so.
June 4, 1965	COMMONS
If I may suggest, Mr. Speaker, a number of the persons who are anxious to do this are new to this House. Some of them have inhabited the rarefied atmosphere of academic institutions and classrooms and others have occupied similar locations. If ever there existed an institution in our society where experience is more necessary than theory, it is the House of Commons. I am sure Your Honour needs no reminding, but I would remind Your Honour that the rules under which we are operating now have grown up not only in this Parliament but in the mother of Parliaments over a period of many hundreds of years. These rules have grown up on the basis of practical experience and they change constantly according to the circumstances.
I think every one of us in this House agrees that because of the increasing complexity of Government in our modern society and because of the various fields into which the Government has now entered which it had not entered a few years ago, the adjustment of these rules is necessary at this time. I do not believe there would be any disagreement on this. It is only a question of the degree to which we wish to change the rules. Naturally, as we have heard during this debate, there are different points of view in this regard. One would expect this in a Parliament made up of 260-odd individual Members, not to mention parties. These views vary depending on which side of the House one sits, whether on the Government side or the Opposition side.
There is one generalization I should like to make and it is this. Many things have been done in human history for the sake of expediency. It is very nice when you are on the Government side of the House-I am one Member who can appreciate this having sat on both sides of the House-to get everything through very quickly and forget the real purposes of Parliament which have been pointed out very ably by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) and yesterday by the hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). The purpose of Parliament is to discuss matters and bring them to public attention. This onus rests particularly on members of the Opposition rather than the Government since, as was well pointed out by previous speakers, the Government usually has the majority on its side as well as the rules.
I believe that one of the things which perhaps precipitated this debate and has led to the introduction of these rule changes by the Government has been the fourth estate or the press. Last summer we had one of the most
DEBATES	1997
House of Commons Procedures lengthy debates we have ever had. Members of the press, not only the Press Gallery here but other people disseminating public information, were very critical of Parliament at that time. Whether or not they were justified is a matter of opinion. I think there is little doubt that the opinions which were expressed as that time through the public information media were badly misinformed. A great many editorials were written and commentaries were made by people who had no understanding at all of Parliament. I should like to say that during this debate those who are responsible for press articles and commentaries on the news have done an excellent job in every respect. This debate has been handled with great seriousness and care as well as thoughtfulness by all those who deal in the various means of disseminating information to the public such as press, television, radio and magazines. I think they have done an extremely good job. However, I believe, rightly or wrongly, that they were largely responsible for pressuring Parliament into introducing these rule changes.
During this debate I believe the varying points of view have been brought a great deal closer. For instance, I believe all of us are agreed upon a limitation of time for the discussion of estimates. I feel it is a great pity that the Government will not accept the suggestion to remove those parts from this resolution on which everyone agrees and let them pass so we can set up the committees on estimates and get on with the business that is supposed to be done. I suppose tactical, political reasons impel the Government to refuse. They want the rest of us to accept the more difficult part of the resolution as well and are attempting to use this as a lever of very unsavory variety. I hope the Government will change its mind so we can get the estimates committees set up and get the business done Parliament is supposed to be doing.
However, there seems to be a tendency amongst many Members of the Government, who are perhaps not really parliamentarians but have been in administrative positions, to lose patience or to lack an understanding of the institution of Parliament. For instance, I would doubt very much-one cannot really know what is going on in another person's mind-that the hon. Member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who is a very distinguished and very able parliamentarian, would entirely agree with all of the arguments his colleagues have been putting forward. I do not expect

Oh, I see. The next point I want to touch on briefly is that most of the contentious points in the resolution before us concern one basic problem, namely, the rights of the majority versus the rights of the minority. It may be safely said that any responsible student or writer of political science and political theory, from the days of Plato down to the present time, would agree that the mark of a truly democratic society is the protection given to minorities. It is certainly a hallmark in our parliamentary democracy to recognize that minorities must be given protection to express their views and thoughts.
I have heard some rather odd views expressed in this regard by Members of the New Democratic Party who have said that the majority, no matter how small, must always have its way absolutely. On reflection I think some of them would think otherwise. On the other hand, I do not think anyone would agree that the wishes of a majority, even a small majority, should be permanently frustrated by a minority, even a big minority, and provided the minority has its proper protection the views of the majority must eventually prevail if, during the process of discussion, they are not changed or altered.
For this reason I think the amendment moved by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) is an excellent one. I for one am entirely opposed to closure for many reasons, some of which I will express in a moment. I know the Government does not call this resolution closure. It says it is an allocation of time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: In view of what he has said about the nature of democracy and his abhorrence of closure, I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he regards the United Kingdom as being other than a democracy?

speechtext: I am delighted to be asked that question and I will deal with it in some detail in a moment. If the hon. Member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) would look a little more closely at what actually takes place in the United Kingdom he might not have asked that question.

The Government's proposal is in fact closure. No matter how thin you slice it, not matter how prettily you dress it up and no matter what you call it, it is still boloney. When I went to high school the authorities always tried to make the algebra book look attractive by putting a red cover on it. It looked very pleasant but to most people that did not disguise its unpleasant content, and the nomenclature that is applied to this proposed rule change, allocation of time for debate, does not disguise what is really going on.
The hon. Member for Antigonish-Guysborough has raised the question of what is done in the United Kingdom. If he would look into the matter he would find that in the 76 years since 1887 when the guillotine, as it is called in the United Kingdom, was introduced, it has been applied to only 57 bills. During the Labour Government from 1945 to 1951 the allocation of time rule was applied to only three bills, and from 1951 to 1962 under the Conservative Government it was applied to nine bills.

speechtext: Would the hon. Member permit a question at this point? Would he agree that the rule he is trying to compare with the proposal now before the House differs in this respect in that our proposal deals with the creation of an all-party committee to deal with the allocation of time and the part of the rule in the United Kingdom that he is talking about deals only with Government action?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I agree there are certain differences between the U.K. rule and the proposed rule changes here and I intend to deal with those in some detail, particularly that aspect referred to by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith). The guillotine rule in the United Kingdom
June 4, 1965

has been applied just over 50 times in less than 100 years, but there it is applied only after debate has begun and after it has been indicated there is going to be a long debate and the business of Parliament is not going to be done.
Here the proposal by the Government is something like Alice in Wonderland. We are going to be asked to limit a debate before it even starts and before we know whether it is going to be contentious. I know the President of the Privy Council may very well say, "Oh yes, but we will have a discussion between the leaders of whatever parties may happen to be in the House." There are five now; there may be six or seven after the next election or two or three. Who knows? But it is made quite clear that if agreement cannot be reached in this Business Committee-I think it will give the Parliament the business all right-then the Minister proposing the legislation in question can invoke this rule.
Though I know the President of the Privy Council and many of his colleagues would not think of such a thing, there are some of his colleagues who would think of something like this, namely, to bring in a nice piece of innocuous legislation that nobody would disagree with, have an agreed time limit and after it is introduced stick in some amendment that would change the whole character of the legislation.
The suggestion has been made that we allow one of the two days debate for this kind of an amendment if the character of the legislation is really changed, and it is left up to Mr. Speaker, whether a permanent Speaker or a continuing Speaker should one eventually be agreed upon, to carry this out. But despite this piece of sugar, which is what it is made to appear, if you completely change the character of legislation and introduce something highly contentious, having agreed in advance on how long the legislation is to be debated, you cannot have anything but the most unpleasant results.
Another thing that can happen with allocation of time was pointed out by the hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) yesterday and by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert today. Since the proposed changes tend more and more to recognize political parties in the House rather than individuals, you would have the political parties deciding who would speak and, as has been so well pointed out by those two members, backbenchers would have little chance to make themselves heard.
House of Commons Procedures
One gets to be a frontbencher by various ways, by being here a long time, by activity in the party and by other ways. We all know this, but in theory at least each constituency in Canada is entitled to one Member of Parliament and each Member of Parliament is entitled to open his mouth in the House to express his constituents' views and raise problems affecting his constituency. If you make rules limiting the time of debate and the question period, then you will have a very queer Parliament indeed where only Members on the front benches and a few others will have a chance to speak. The poor backbencher on the Government side and on the Opposition side will be denied this opportunity.

This, I think, is improper. However, others in this House have different views and we must try to reach some accommodation.
Consider the suggestions which have been made that the question period be limited. I realize that since 1955 or 1956 the question period has become longer and longer. Many of the questions asked, I think we would all agree, are neither urgent nor of national importance as they ought to be. If there is criticism of Parliament by the public and the press I think the question period is a period to which those criticisms might well be directed. I do not think there is one Member in this House who is not guilty. This is an aspect of our procedure which could be reviewed, but if we try to set a time limit upon the question period every day of the week the same thing will happen. Those who speak on behalf of their parties or who sit on the front benches will have advantages which backbenchers are denied. Further, Ministers who are invited to answer questions will spin out the answers as long as they can in order to avoid further questions being asked. No doubt a number of questions will be "planted" and asked by supporters of the Government so that the Opposition may not be able to ask many. This is what is likely to happen. However, we shall have to reach some agreement, I suppose, and I hope that when the time comes the Government will be prepared to allow one day a week when the question period is unlimited.

Member for York-Scarborough asked me whether I did not think that limitation of time was implicit in the amendment suggested by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert. I do not approve of closure in any form. After all, Members of this House are paid $18,000 a year and if we sit all year round what difference does it make to our constituents as long as we get through our business? If we have to sit throughout the year to get the nation's business done, let us do it. Apparently everyone here does not think that way, so we have to reach some kind of compromise. The Government insists on bringing in this provision for the allocation of time and apparently it has some support from other quarters. Let us try to reach an agreement or consensus which is half way between the two points of view.
My hon. friend from Saint John-Albert suggested that this proposed order could only be applied if 60 per cent of the Members present in the House agreed. Everyone tends to think of these rules in terms of Parliament as it is today when there are five parties in the House and the Government is in a minority position. If the President of the Privy Council and those of his colleagues who have the responsibility for making decisions will look at this proposal they will see that it does not give the Opposition a veto power over the Government at all. The Official Opposition would have to be supported by at least one of the other parties in the House and it is difficult for the Government to argue that if two of the Opposition parties oppose the rule there is not something wrong with its application. I think it is a safeguard for the Opposition as well as for the Government. If this amendment were accepted it would not be possible for any one of the Opposition parties to frustrate the wishes of the Government. On the other hand, if the Government were making a mistake, which has been known to happen, and two of the Opposition parties combined to object to this rule, the rule could not apply. I do not think this is at all unreasonable.
I realize there are others who would like to speak on this question and I do not propose to take any more time. I trust the President of the Privy Council and those who assisted him in drawing up these proposed changes will give consideration to exactly what this allocation of time rule or closure rule really involves. It means closure before a debate

Mr. Speaker, I cannot for the life of me understand how I can deal with this important matter without referring to those factors which resulted in the situation in which Parliament finds itself today, a situation in respect of which the Prime Minister says we must change the rules in order to correct it. All I am trying to do is present evidence in respect of what happened and what effect this has had on the length of Parliament and the efficient handling of the business of the House.
I referred to the code of ethics not because I wanted to delve into that particular matter but because of what that indicates has happened during the last two years here in the House of Commons. I look over at the ministerial benches and find gifted men, university professors and trained successful businessmen, most of them handpicked by the Prime Minister himself. If the image of Parliament had not been tarnished before, certainly when the Prime Minister found it necessary to issue a code of ethics to these people it became tarnished. That in itself could not help but bring into question the whole image of Parliament.
A great deal of the time of this House has been consumed, Sir, as you well know, by Opposition Members of all parties asking questions of the ministry. If the Prime Minister had not been so secretive and if his Ministers had been more frank and less reluctant to give facts we might now have a different situation.
The Department of the Minister of Justice has almost become a pawn in the political survival of that party. The Prime Minister has shut his eyes and ears to these improprieties. Parliament has suffered first of all because of secretiveness on the part of the Prime Minister, who now interprets his duty to individual friends as being greater than his responsibility to the nation as a whole. The Minister of Justice has made that very plain in his attitude toward questions asked recently by the hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
The Minister of Justice has now been shorn of his duties as House Leader and has been replaced by the very able and amiable Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). That hon. gentleman has been given the task by the Prime Minister of convincing Parliament and the Canadian people, through the resolu-
June 4, 1965

tion changing the rules and procedures of the house, that the rules as they now stand have been the cause of all the Government's troubles.
Why should an individual Member of Parliament, whether in the Government or in the Opposition, be denied full and free access to this assembly in order that he may represent his people, because of the carelessness of those who sit opposite? That is the price the Government is trying to exact to save the day for its own party. I suggest to you, Sir, that this is a questionable manoeu-ver. The problem now faced is not one for Parliament to solve but one for the people of Canada to decide. Our task is to ensure proper and full opportunity for even the newest Member of the House of Commons to speak freely during the debates of this House, to preserve for the individual Member the right to be heard regardless of party policy at any particular time.
I recall the days when my leader, the hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenba-ker), was the Prime Minister, particularly because there were occasions then when I thought it necessary to place before the House views that were not entirely in agreement with those of the party to which I belonged. Had the policies now adopted by the Government been in effect at that time I would then have had to cross the floor to the Opposition side in order to be heard. I shudder to think of the consequences and disappointment had that eventuality occurred.
We are not elected to the House of Commons as parties; we are elected by constituents to represent them. Indeed, it has always been my understanding that once elected one should not represent only those who supported him but all his constituents. The rights of individual Members in this House should be our main consideration and those rights are of fundamental consideration in a democracy.
All of us have watched the embarrassment and confusion of the Prime Minister and the Government which have grown from day to day. I say to you, Sir, that that is no licence for this Prime Minister and his Government to attempt to curtail debate and the right of the individual Member to the floor of the House of Commons.
We know there are certain restraints in effect today and there is hardly a Member of this House who has not prepared notes for a speech which he has not delivered. We have adopted these self-disciplinary meas-

If we are going to make the rules so stringent that only a party viewpoint is going to be presented, then it will not be long before the House of Commons will be filled with independents or with even more minority groups than we have at the present time.
It has always been my belief that access to the floor of the House to speak your mind even when it differs from the viewpoint of your party, with the possibility of still remaining within your party, is important. Possibly one of the greatest dangers of the changes now contemplated lies in the encouragement which would be given to independent Members and to a multiplicity of parties which would lead to the prolongation of debates and the minority position that we find in this Parliament with all its attendant handicaps for the orderly dispatch of business.
If we want to reform our rules why do we not take a look at the way we vote in this House? We should take a look at the time that is lost whenever a vote is called. This is one of the things that has been ignored by those who drafted these rule changes. I believe that the provision of an all-party committee to discuss the allocation of time will result in Parliament talking about procedure rather than dealing with the problems that face us.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the amendment that has been brought forward by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. 

Bell) which makes a serious proposal to the effect that if the Government is going to pursue its destructive policy in so far as the rights of Parliament are concerned it should at least not be able to have its will in this regard until at least 60 per cent of the Members of the House have approved. When this debate began it commenced on a very high level which was established by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who indicated that they agreed that reform of Parliament was necessary. At the same time, both of these distinguished speakers pointed out that if we were going to move forward as a Parliament and come to any agreement as to the form these reforms should take, then it could only be done in a spirit of compromise. This spirit of compromise prevailed up until the time when we reached the impasse of the past few days on the Government's insistence on bringing about closure by indirection.
The whole idea of the reform of Parliament is not a new one. We have been gradually moving forward over the years that I have been in the House in the direction of amending our rules and changing our procedures, thereby gradually adapting to the changes made necessary by our changing economic and social circumstances as well as by the actual situation that exists in this House. When I first came to Parliament in 1951 there was absolutely no allocation of time. I think we have come a long way because now we do accept allocation of time on the important, major debates such as the Throne Speech and the budget debate as well as specified time limits with regard to certain formal speeches. In 1951, which was the first session I attended, there was no allocation of time on the Throne Speech debate. I can recall being rather shocked-yes, I think I could use that term- when the debate dragged on for almost a month. We now wind up that debate in the comparatively short time of one week.
The reforms to which many speakers have rcferrsd have come about as a natural adjustment to the changing circumstances of the country and the changing circumstances which exist in this House. I do not need to go further because they have been well covered. As I indicated in my opening remarks, I want to give reasons for my support of the amendment brought forward by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert this afternoon. These reforms have been necessitated by the

presence of multiple parties in the house. This has led to successive minority Governments. These reforms have been necessitated also by the fact that we are faced with problems of increased complexity in the nation. I should like to reinforce the fundamental point that has been raised by many speakers during this debate, that the solution to the increasing complexity of problems with which this Parliament has to deal is not necessarily turning Parliament into a time machine or automaton.

I have been rather shocked by the misconceptions certain Government spokesmen seem to have with reference to the functions of Parliament. They talk about streamlining, getting on with the business of the Plouse, and making Parliament effective. Again I stress that shortcuts rather than having increased the efficiency of the House in the past usually became shortcuts to tyranny and authoritarianism.
It has been the history of all experiments in democracy that complexity in Government invariably leads to the abuse of power. I recall debates in this House on the difficulty that has arisen because of the fact that as a result of the growing complexity the executive arm of the Government, which after all is responsible for carrying on the business of the nation, has become so badly bogged down that even its power has been transferred from the floor of the House of Commons to the offices of the bureaucrats. More and more we have seen this unhappy situation develop.
The real reason for my supporting this amendment, which says that an allocation of time must have the approval of 60 per cent of the Members of the House, is that the Government is a bureaucraticminded one, something which inevitably results from the presence of numerous bureaucrats within its ranks.
In this connection I quote the remarks made by the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) as recorded at page 1,942 of yesterday's Hansard:

It is a Government which has been stereotyped by a spirit of arrogance for a long time in this nation. If we limit debate beyond the extent to which concessions have already been made by compromise, I feel that Parliament as we know it will be in great jeopardy. If we take this further step, private Members of the House will certainly need greater assistance than they have had up to the present time. They will need expanded research facilities. We must bear in mind the attitude which the Government has taken toward the discussion of public affairs freely and openly in this House. Even during the question period when we seek information on public policy the attitude of the Treasury Bench is one which favours obscuring these issues rather than throwing light on the questions involved.
I make this final plea which has been made by many hon. Members during this discussion: Let us continue in the spirit of compromise which has marked this debate until the last few days. We have agreed on major concessions. Members of the Official Opposition have agreed to make major concessions. My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has even proposed that we should pass the non-controversial proposals, set up the committees and enable them to start work on the business to be referred to them. We heartily agree that the committee system should be used so as to avoid unnecessary and repetitious discussion in this House. But let us not, by attempting to resolve our difficulties by shortcuts, take the road to tyranny in this country.
What the Government now proposes should not be done unless the suggestion put forward in good faith by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) with reference to a continuing or permanent Speaker is accepted. Members on the other side of the House have referred to the British system and the way in which time is allocated in the British Parliament. But they have failed to note that it is the Speaker, an independent Speaker, a permanent Speaker, who has the final say in deciding whether a motion for allocation of time is to be presented to the House. If we are to be railroaded in this fashion the minimum requirement will have to be the provision of a permanent Speaker in this House.
Again, those who have referred to the British practice have failed to mention that there is always uneasiness in the British Parliament on the rare occasions when the

limitation of time provision is resorted to. As I read the discussions there, there is a feeling that because it violates the fundamental rights of Members of the House it is necessary to bring about some modification of the right application of that system.
The most striking example of rigid allocation of time for the consideration of public issues comes from the Soviet Union. There they are able to handle parliamentary discussion of business in a matter of weeks. The time limit is so absolute that the assembly has become a body that exists virtually to give formal approval to the executive arm which, of course, has authoritarian power. Let us not, even with the best of intentions, follow that example. Many have said that the intentions of the Government in this regard are of the purest, that they want to get on with the business of the nation. If that is so, let the Cabinet, the executive arm of Parliament, prepare its legislation more carefully so that its bills need not be put forward and then withdrawn three or four times. Let it allow the ordinary Members of this House freedom of expression and freedom to express the point of view of the people they represent when public issues are raised in this chamber.

I would open my remarks, however, by expressing my regret once again that the Government has now reached a position where it is being adamant and is refusing to budge. I feared this would happen when I first saw the resolution on the order paper. Bearing in mind the conciliatory tone of the Prime Minister's speech I thought that perhaps some modification would result and that we would not reach a deadlock on an item which was known at the time to be extremely controversial. Today I again asked the Prime Minister if he would set aside the controversial item now before the House in the hope that we might proceed to approve of 90 per cent of the various proposals embodied in the two resolutions. I thought the House would speedily do this. Again my request was refused.
I am gradually losing confidence in the answers the Prime Minister gives to many things. When I asked him today whether he would set aside that portion of the resolution
House of Commons Procedures which deals with the new closure rule his reply-and I copied down his words-was as follows: "There is, of course, no new closure rule under discussion. There are rules to allocate times to proposed legislation which comes before the House." I submit, Sir, that this statement of the Prime Minister is misleading. When he says that there is no new closure rule under discussion, I say that the Prime Minister is ignorant of what is being proposed in the resolution which he put before this House because this is a form of closure. Other people who have spoken in the course of the debate have indicated that, even such a close supporter of the Government as the hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) who, as reported at page 1544 of Hansard, used these words:

The proposed standing order 15A is really another type of guillotine, a more refined type of guillotine.
"Guillotine" and "closure" are the customary words used in connection with the arbitrary and forceful closing off of freedom of speech in the House of Commons. So when the Prime Minister says there is no new closure rule under discussion, I say that statement is misleading. I hope it was not calculated to mislead the public; I hope it was made through ignorance of what is being considered.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us consider exactly what we mean by "closure". We have Standing Order 33, and the marginal note calls it "Closure". I think it would be advantageous to see how that rule compares with the one now being considered by the House. I think if a person looks closely at the two he will see that the new proposal is a form of closure. Standing Order 33 reads as follows:
Immediately before the order of the day for resuming an adjourned debate is called, or if the House be in committee of the whole, or of supply, or of ways and means, any Minister of the Crown who, standing in his place, shall have given notice at a previous sitting of his intention so to do, may move that the debate shall not be further adjourned, or that the further consideration of any resolution or resolutions, clause or clauses, section or sections, preamble or preambles, title or titles, shall be the first business of the committee, and shall not further be postponed: and in either case such question shall be decided without debate or amendment: and if the same shall be resolved in the affirmative, no member shall thereafter speak more than once, or longer than twenty minutes in any such adjourned debate; or, if in committee, on any such resolution, clause, section, preamble or title: and if such adjourned debate or postponed consideration shall not have been resumed or concluded before one o'clock in the morning, no member shall rise to speak after that hour, but all such questions as

House of Commons Procedures must be decided in order to conclude such adjourned debate or postponed consideration, shall be decided forthwith.
Consider, Sir, the resemblance between that and the proposed new closure rule. In the present rule notice has to be given by a Minister. When the motion then comes before the House it is decided without debate or amendment and once it has been decided in the affirmative the House enters into a limited period of debate which concludes at one o'clock in the morning with each Member being restricted to 20 minutes. The new, proposed closure rule varies this to a certain extent. If the Business Committee fails to reach agreement, the new closure rule may be in-introduced by a Minister. The new closure rule will permit one day's debate, at which time the vote must be called to decide whether the new closure rule shall be put into effect. If this is resolved in the affirmative, the debate on the legislation then before the House is restricted in time. There are slight modifications; it is not to be under two days for second reading, two days for committee and one day for third reading. But there is a definite closure imposed.
The new rule as amended this morning gives the Government spokesman an opportunity to restrict, in the course of the various divisions of that general debate, the rights of private Members with regard to time. It could be 20 minutes, 10 minutes, 5 minutes or 30 minutes, but there is a restriction of time for speaking involved in the new closure rule. Let me indicate this, Sir. It has been pointed out to us time and time again that the new, proposed closure rule is an adaptation of a rule in force in England which is called allocation of time. We have had presented to us an argument that this is just an orderly arrangement of debate and follows a recognized British practice. I have pointed out that the recognized British practice has almost fallen into abeyance over the years and is rarely used. The authority on the British rules and procedure is Sir Erskine May, and in his sixteenth edition of "Parliamentary Practice" at pages 476 and 477, dealing with this subject, you find these words:
In such circumstances-
This is when the Government has decided that debate must be restricted:
-resort is had sooner or later-
I ask you, Sir, to listen to these words:
-to the most drastic method of curtailing debate known to procedure, namely the allocation of a specified number of days to the various stages of

a bill, and (in the case of the committee and report stages) of limited amounts of time to particular portions of the bill, together with provision for securing the disposal of the stages or portions of the bill at the end of the time allotted for each. This method is not provided for by the standing orders but is applied, when the need arises, by special orders of the House, known officially as "Allocation of Time" orders, and colloquially as "Guillotine" or "Closure by compartment" orders.
In other words, in the British practice this is called "closure by compartment" or "guillotine". I will read on:
The provisions of these orders are described in detail in the third section of this chapter. They may be regarded as the extreme limit to which procedure goes in affirming the rights of the majority at the expense of the minorities of the House, and it cannot be denied that they are capable of being used in such a way as to upset the balance, generally so carefully preserved, between the claims of business and the rights of debate.
The proposal now before the Canadian House of Commons is an adaptation of "closure by compartment" as it is called in England, or "guillotine". I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is another form of closure and that the Prime Minister is quite incorrect in saying that closure is not the subject before the House of Commons. He said that no new closure rule was under discussion. I say the Prime Minister is wrong and that he is misleading the House and the public when he uses those words, because the closure rule is under discussion and it is an adaptation of closure in England which is called "closure by compartment", "guillotine" or sometimes "allocation of time". The three terms are used and it is closure, closure of debate. It is a limitation on debate and it is similar to our Standing Order 33 which is a limitation on debate because under Standing Order 33 we have one day in which to conclude the debate and each Member is restricted to 20 minutes.

It is rather strange that we should have to do this in view of the statement of the Prime Minister. When he was talking earlier about the necessity, as he saw it, for making alterations in the rules he spoke, and quite eloquently, about the functions of the Government and of the Opposition. It functions, in other words, in defence of and criticism of the Government and the Executive. The essence of democracy is that the defence and the criticism are equally important. They are together the process by which guidance and warning is given to the direction of our national affairs. The House of Commons is where the primary defence of Government policy must be made, and where the primary attack on Government policy should be made.
Just a little further on, when speaking about the possible decline in the value of Parliament, he says:
The first decline becomes apparent, and dangerous, when a majority rides rough-shod over the strong views, sincerely held, of a minority-
I represent a minority. I hold strong views, which are sincerely held, with regard to this further unnecessary closure rule that the Government is trying to introduce. That is why I am speaking again today. I think it is wrong. I think it will contribute to a decline in the parliamentary system and it runs counter to those noble words:
The essence of democracy is that the defence and the criticism are equally important.
To avoid criticism the Government puts on the closure rule. What about the essence of

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill I am introducing today, seconded by my good friend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn), is to amend an old statute under which the first day of July was designated as our national holiday under the name of "Dominion Day", so as to give it a name more in keeping with the present status of our country by calling it "Canada Day".
The first of July should be considered by all Canadians as the ideal day on which to take stock of our achievements during the year gone by. So, everyone must be made to understand that this day is that of our national holiday and it must have a truly Canadian character. It is a day on which our citizenship must be emphasized, as well as our pride in being able to live in so beautiful a country.
Every year since I have been sitting in this house, I noticed with regret that the first of July was not designated the same way throughout the country, and when some members asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) what was the official designation of our national holiday, I became somewhat irritated, like most of you. Some refer to it as "Dominion Day" or "jour du Dominion"; others, as "Canada Day" or "jour du Canada"; others, as "Confederation Day" or "jour de la Confederation"; others, as merely the first of July.
Since the Statute of Westminster, it is obvious that the word "dominion" does not apply as much because, in fact, we are no longer a

dominion. May I quote two experts in that field.
First, Mr. Maurice Ollivier, that distinguished jurist well known to hon. members, in his book "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty", said this:
The statute of Westminster was, therefore, the confirmation of Balfour's statement at the 1926 Imperial Conference to the effect that the dominions had become autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
May I also mention a remark made by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King on the word "dominion":
The least one can say about such a usage is that it leads to confusion, when it is not to misunderstanding and misinterpretation of the facts. South Africa is South Africa; New Zealand is New Zealand; Australia is Australia and Canada is Canada.
Therefore, I think it is very desirable to give a more uniform and more acceptable character to that national holiday. That is why I propose in this bill to call our national holiday, that of all Canadians regardless of their ethnic origin, Canada Day.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that a similar bill was passed on April 4, 1946, and that at that time, many members who still are here, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, (Mr. Knowles) voted in favour of that bill. It was then sent to the Senate which adopted it with a slight amendment.
I would also point out that the provision concerning the Canada Day was exactly the same as that I am suggesting today. Unfortunately, the session having ended too soon, the house could not examine that amendment, and the bill was automatically removed from the order paper.
Therefore, due to the confusion which exists throughout the country, and considering that it is necessary to create an essentially Canadian day and ensure the uniformity of such a symbol, I believe that the day of every Canadian should be called immediately Canada Day.
I hope that the house will pass this piece of legislation. I know that my colleagues on this side of the House approve of it, and I hope that those who wish to speak about it do so as concisely as possible, so that the matter may be put to a vote.
