Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. Member on the manner of his presentation, but let me say at the outset that I disagree completely, thoroughly, wholeheartedly, emotionally and intellectually with its content. I cannot see how we make our Canadianism more meaningful, how we become more truly Canadian, and I am paraphrasing some of his remarks, by dropping from our vocabulary, and from the designation of our national day one of the unique contributions which our country has made to the whole of political terminology, namely, the word "Dominion".
Because a thing is old does not make it useless. On the other hand, I think because a thing is old does not mean that there should not and could not be proper and valuable reasons for change. The word "Dominion" is something of which I am very proud. I think its origin might, instead of being glossed over, be looked into a little more carefully.
I have before me a copy of a letter from the son of one of the great Fathers of Confederation, Sir Leonard Tilley. He writes:
You state that you have heard and read that my father, the late Sir S. L. Tilley, was the one who suggested this name. You are correct in this statement as far as my knowledge goes. I have heard my father state how he came to suggest it at the B.N.A. Conference. When the Fathers of Confederation were assembled discussing the terms and conditions of Confederation and the drafting of the British North America Act there had been considerable discussion the day before and many suggestions as to what the new United Canada should be called, and no conclusion had been reached.
Apparently there were delays at that time too. They were politicians, after all.
The discussion on the name stood over until the next day. The next morning, as was Sir Leonard's custom-
He was a good Maritimer.
-he read a chapter from the Bible, and that that particular morning he read Psalm 72, Verse 8, "He shall have Dominion also from sea to sea." When reading verse 8 of the said Psalm, the thought occurred to him, what a splendid name to give Canada, the word "Dominion" of Canada. When he went back to the sitting of the convention that morning he suggested the word "Dominion", which was agreed to, and Canada was called the "Dominion of Canada".
Thus we have great meaning attached to our Latin motto: A Mari Usque Ad Mare- from the sea all the way to the sea. The name has more than a religious significance, it has historical significance in that it represents the political thinking that was taking place at the time. The Fathers of Confederation wanted, and they said this, to build

American delegates are anxious that the United provinces should be designated as the Dominion of Canada".
The word "Dominion" is a great word and if I was not limited to 20 minutes and liked to read statutes and statistics, I could point out hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of times where the word "Dominion" appears in the statutes of this Parliament. That is legal usage and it is proper and by chance, indeed, it happens also to be a French word, although archaic French as the dictionary points out.
The hon. Member referred to the Statute of Westminster. That Statute in my opinion does not constitute an argument for discarding this historic word but merely updates it. It indicates that at that stage of our political development, a political development which this country pioneered, the Dominion was defined, as the hon. gentleman quoted so well, as an autonomous community in a free political society.
The Statute of Westminster itself refers to the word "Dominion" many, many times. The second line of it, I may say, refers to "Dominion of Canada", and the Statute refers to it 30 times thereafter. The Statute of Westminster cannot be brought in support of this retrograde and unhistoric step.

I do not know if this is documented and perhaps it would be difficult to document, but someone who was observing the attempts of the Mackenzie King-St. Laurent Government to adopt and extend the word "Federal" said the one thing that stopped them dead in their tracks was the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The dropping of the first "D" would leave a very undesirable implication.
More important, I am concerned with the fact that today we live not in the day of the nationalists but the denationalists. The concept of the Dominion, the entity, is not of a whole of which others are a part but more and more one of 11 Governments that sit down to negotiate and discuss, invariably to the advantage of the ten and not the senior Government. In this day of the denationalists, I think we would be well advised to recall that the whole is greater than the parts and that there are many things which must be done, not only by political institutions but all of the people, to give their allegiance to the whole. When people are afraid of the word "Nation" or "Nations", how sound, how sensible to designate the political entity which was created nearly a hundred years ago by the word "Dominion". Those who were French and those who were not French created one of the great, successful experiments when people of different cultures, different religions, moved together and built something

that was good, something that was great, that was lasting.
It is said we must not leave the word "Dominion" because we confuse people. I wonder that the French do not change the name July 14 from Bastille Day to France Day, and why the Irish do not ask for an Ireland Day. How much would we advance anything by the passage of such a measure as this? If there is anyone in Canada who does not know what Dominion means or what Dominion of Canada means, I think it behooves those of us who are interested in our future and in our children to do something about it. One of the great facts of our country is that we are so afraid to enthuse about our history, about our historical figures. As a result of our fear of glamourizing something, we play it down so much that we found when we discussed the flag some time ago we had not really thought very much about these things. The significance of them had not entered into our minds, into our souls. Heaven knows, this country is not over-blessed with interest in its history. We have done our part in ignoring the past, so let us in this instance look upon this word as something which binds us all together, we from the Maritimes and the hon. Member from Quebec. The creation of the Dominion was a great uniting experience in statescraft, no group dominating the other, no groups with special privileges, but all areas contributing and working together.

This is a time in our history when there is a searching for symbols to indicate just what is Canada. The symbols include such things as a flag, which we tortuously found last year, such things as an anthem or a song to symbolize what Canada is, such things as names established and applied to a particular day during which we can fleetingly look back, remember and think about our history and the meaning of Canada.
It is a fact that the greatest, most intense, and certainly the most vocal demand for such symbols emanates from the province of Quebec. Others in other parts of the nation

are interested, but the Members from the province of Quebec are perhaps more vocal in expressing their desires to find these particular symbols. In part I think this arises because of a sort of massive, cultural inferiority complex, but regardless of the reasons for propounding or proposing certain symbols we cannot delude ourselves into thinking that these symbols will make us proud of ourselves or that they will make Canadians more proud of being Canadian. In fact just the reverse is true. It is what we think of our nation and ourselves that makes the symbols worth while.
I, for instance, am just as proud and will be just as proud and honoured to be a Canadian privileged to have been born in this nation whether we call the 1st of July Dominion day, Canada day, simply the 1st of July or some other equally appropriate name. What we should be doing is trying to unwind ourselves from our blind dedication to the past and see if we cannot, through the establishment of symbols, grow into adulthood. If in this process of growing up it is necessary to change the name Dominion Day to Canada Day, then I am all for it. I am willing to give it a try.
Since I was born, the 1st of July in my memory and in my family's use of it has always been Dominion Day. Other people think historically and traditionally of it, almost from the time they are in knee pants, as simply being the 1st of July. But surely we should be prepared to forget, not to drive out of our memories entirely but to forget a bit of our own personal upbringing in our desire to find some symbols of which we can truly be proud in the years ahead. For these reasons I generally support the bill before us.
However, I think this should have been a subject matter which the Government itself should have introduced and which it should have been proud to introduce. I ofttimes think that in matters such as this, where there may be some delicacy involved and where feelings may be upset, the Government deliberately takes the course of getting one of its backbenchers to introduce a bill, such as was the case with the changing of the name of Trans-Canada Air Lines, so that the Government can take the credit if the bill passes and can blame somebody else in case there is a great public outcry.

Mr. Speaker, first I am pleased to congratulate the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) for introducing this bill and, second, I

wish to thank him for allowing me to have the pleasure and the honour of seconding it. As the hon. Member has stated, on April 4, 1946 a similar bill was debated and passed by the House. As he also stated, it went to the Senate and because of the end of the session the amendments could not be passed so that the bill died.
I am hoping that this bill today will not die. I am hoping that today this bill will pass. Many of us on this side of the House are in favour of letting it pass and for that reason I am only going to speak briefly in the hope that the bill will not be talked out.
I favour the bill for two main reasons. In the first place, to me the word "dominion" in the present act is outdated. The Statute of Westminster, as the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche indicated, confirmed our position as a free and independent nation. We are equal to all; we are subservient to none. We are loyal to the Crown; we are free and happy partners in the Commonwealth.
We have dominion over no one, and none has dominion over us.
Hear, hear.

This leads me to my second point. I believe we should be proud of our state as an independent, free nation. I have felt for many, many years that we Canadians have lacked national pride. We have been very diffident about our Canadianism. Comparing our attitudes to our country with those of people in other lands, and I think in particular of the people to the south of us, we have been very hesitant about expressing our views and sentiments about our country.
The hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has a slightly different view from mine about the meaning and importance of symbols. I believe that symbols can be important as a focal point for our feelings of pride in our country and that by reason of the fact that they exist they do help us to express, concentrate and develop this pride in our country. I therefore welcome the idea of calling our national holiday Canada Day.
I think this is going to help us express our pride in our country. I think it will help us express this pride to ourselves and to people outside our country. Let us do as we do now. Let us celebrate our loyalty to the Crown. Let us celebrate our partnership in the Commonwealth on May 24. But let us celebrate our own country; let us celebrate Canada on Canada Day, July the 1st.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this bill. I am

afraid I did not examine the Order Paper closely enough to realize it was going to come up for debate on this occasion. But I do want to express my opinions regarding this bill. I think I would be in default if I did not do so.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I have considerable regard for the hon. Member who introduced this measure and for the speech he made on it but I do not believe that reasoning, however correct the process may be, can be accepted if it is based on false premises. Part of the difficulty arises,
I think, from the fact that the word "dominion" is not properly translated from English into French. I say this although I am not a linguist able to express an authoritative opinion on the matter. I do not believe the word has the same shade of meaning in the English language as it has in the French language. There may even be areas in the world where the interpretation of the English word is not the same as is generally the case. It is common knowledge that many words in the English language have taken on other shades of meaning when used in different areas of the world.
To me the word "dominion" has the meaning given to it in the Oxford dictionary-a territory or domain. In other words, it means an area which is under one Government, that is, a country; in other words, it is an area populated by people who are governed by one Government. There may be shades of meaning or overtones of some sort of subservience in the usage of the word in the French language and presumably in Toronto, if I followed the hon. Member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) correctly. But to most English speaking people and at least to me it has no connotation of this sort whatsoever. The word "dominion" is one which it would seem to me people should be proud to attach to their country or to their Government or to emanations of that Government.
Having said this, I want to go back almost 100 or even 100 years to the period when the union of the colonies of what was then known as British North America was contemplated. At that time there were in existence Upper and Lower Canada, which had been united under one Government for some time as Canada, and there were the colonies, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia which were at various times parties to these discussions. As everyone knows, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the two Canadas were the colonies which formed the dominion in the first instance.

When the question of what to call this confederation arose, it was known to be a contentious one. Those responsible wanted to evolve a name which would give a new breath of understanding to anyone who referred to this union. It was no longer to be called Canada only. We recall that in those days Canada was a limited area. In very general terms it comprised the watershed of the St. Lawrence River system. The other colonies were never known as Canada. Indeed, they had no connection with Canada. Canada at that time was just as foreign to them as Bermuda or the West Indies. As a matter of fact the part of the country from which I come was much more intimate socially and economically with the West Indies and with Bermuda than with the Canada of that day. The trade of the Atlantic provinces, as they later became, flowed north and south by water. But having decided to enter this confederation they regarded the question of the name as being an important one.
As I have said, the name "Canada" had no application whatever to the Atlantic colonies at that time. Even I, and I do not consider myself really ancient, can remember old people who regarded anyone leaving for Toronto or Quebec as going away to a foreign country. They were going to Canada. And I suppose in still more recent times it was difficult for people in Newfoundland to realize that it was no longer necessary to leave Newfoundland to be in Canada.
In discussing the name of the new federation one of the names put forward was "Newfoundland". After all, the whole of the region was a new-found land. The term "Newfoundland" was applied in the first instance, in any case, to a great area of North America; it became applicable to one particular island only at a later date.
Would the hon. Member permit a question? Is he suggesting that it might be a good idea to change the name "Canada" to "Newfoundland"?

I think it is a bit
late to do that, but I certainly would not have had much objection to it at the time of which I am speaking. I think it would have been a better choice in the first instance. Probably one of the difficulties was that Newfoundland did not enter confederation at that early period. That probably put the suggestion out of court to begin with.
The Fathers of Confederation were striving to find a name which would not be limited in its application to the area of the St.

Lawrence watershed. It must be remembered that the term "Canada" at that date was applied to only a small part of what are now the Provinces of Quebec and Ontario. In 1912 vast northern territories were added to each of these two provinces. There was naturally some resentment among the people of the Maritimes provinces to the new country being called simply "Canada". For one thing the term did not attach any significance to the entry into confederation of some of the colonies. There was the danger that the impression would develop among the people of the Canadas-I think that such an impression did, unfortunately, come into being and it still exists-that they were simply acquiring some appendages to widen their borders. If the word "Canada" alone were used it was feared they would not become fully aware of the fact that this was a brand new country of vast extent the meaning of which could not be expressed by the term "Canada" as it was used in those days.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Suggestions such as the country might be called "Assiniboia" were put forward by some. Assiniboia was a vast territory in what is now called Western Canada. There were no doubt many other suggestions. But as a compromise it was decided to call the new country the "Dominion of Canada," from the biblical quotation given by my colleague, to make people realize that it was no longer the small, ingrown, parochial area of the St. Lawrence watershed but a great country stretching from sea to sea. That is what the word "Dominion" attached to "Canada" is supposed to connote.

It was the "Dominion of Canada".

speechtext: And section 5.
I agree with that, Mr. Speaker. I am not questioning it. But it was also decided as a compromise-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. Member permit me to ask him a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is it not true that the word "Dominion" was devised to replace the word "Kingdom" in "Kingdom of Canada", which it was thought at the time was not acceptable to the Americans?
I think that was a proposal that was put forward by Sir John A. Macdonald and this was substituted by the word "Dominion".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: So that the word "Dominion" has a general meaning, as the hon. Member said at the beginning of his remarks, and could be used anywhere. The word "Dominion" is not peculiar to Canada but the word "Canada" is peculiar to Canada.

That is right; but the word "Dominion" was used to differentiate between Canada as it was known in those days and this new country, this new confederation of a group of colonies coming together. The word "Dominion" is not entirely unique so far as Canada is concerned; you also have the Dominion of New Zealand, for example. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the retention of "Dominion" should still apply, so we can get away from this narrow, parochial view that only the St. Lawrence Valley is Canada. Canada is a far greater concept than it was 100 years ago, so much greater that it bears no resemblance to the Canada of that day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. Member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. Member if it is not true that in modern usage the parts of British North America which were formerly referred to as Upper and Lower Canada are now referred to as Ontario and Quebec? I should also like to ask the hon. Member whether the term "Dominion" has not in our usage, both popular and constitutional, come to take its meaning from a particular period in our constitutional development, namely, the period of "Dominion status"?

I do not think this is entirely valid, Mr. Speaker. As I said at the beginning, there are more meanings than one or more shades of meaning to the word "Dominion". One of them is a country that is governed by one government, over which a government has control. As far as the status of the country is concerned, maybe the term "Dominion status" was very unfortunate. Nevertheless, there is nothing in the usage of the word "Dominion" to indicate that we are subservient to anybody else. Nothing in the word "Dominion" is contrary to our having complete and utter self-determination as a country. I believe the same is true of New Zealand.
In the documents printed in the British North America Act and Selected Statutes, 1867-1948, issued by the King's Printer, 1948, the term "Dominion of Canada" occurs 153 times, "Union or Dominion of Canada" 18 times, "Union of the Dominion of Canada" twice, "the said Dominion" or "our said Dominion" 46 times, and so on. "Dominion of Canada" alone or in combination occurs 173 times. In 103 of the cases it was used, not by the British Government or Parliament or officials, who might perhaps be supposed not to know what was what, but by our own Parliament which certainly ought to have known and which started doing it in 1869 and kept it up till 1948. "Dominion" in some other form occurs 319 times, and again in 220 cases, ranging from 1869 to 1945, our own Parliament was the culprit. Whatever the notion may be in some areas, Mr. Speaker, at the present time it is perfectly obvious that when the colonies of British North America agreed to confederate the name "Dominion of Canada" was a compromise as far as the colonies other than the Canada of the day were concerned. It was

to indicate that this was not just a grandi-osement of the Canada of the day but was a new concept for a new country, a new confederation stretching from sea to sea.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say that I am certainly not in favour of switching our "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day". I am convinced that Canada as a virile nation, a nation that is going places in the world, does not need to work into every phase of its life the word "Canada." I believe that when in the past Canadians have gone abroad they have given a picture of Canada that is second to none in the world. To me this business of changing the name from "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day" is going to weaken this particular day, because we already have Canada, everybody knows we have Canada, and we have Canadians.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

"Dominion Day" to my mind speaks of something much richer than just "Canada Day". "Canada Day" is a cold expression. It expresses the name of our country, but Dominion Day to me is a more neighbourly expression used in connection with a celebration which embraces all those united peoples having dominion over the whole area in which they live as a community and as a family.
Someone said that the word "Dominion" was not peculiar to the United States. The United States celebrates its Independence Day, as do several nations in the world. I say we should not weaken our position and take away from any people in the country the deeper meaning of our celebration day by changing Dominion Day to Canada Day.
I am reminded of the preacher who had as a side note to his sermon the words "Holler loud because your argument is weak", and I think this applies here. We are putting "Air Canada" on our aircraft because air travel is international and our aircraft fly routes which take them far from the borders of our country. I do not say this is wrong, but an erosion is going on here of some of the traditions which make Canada what it is.
We have been here for 100 years. In those 100 years we have developed traditions and history. One of these days there will be an attempt to do away with the words "Royal Mail" and to change them to "Canada Mail". Everybody knows it is Canada mail.

And why not?

There go the Republicans.
This sort of erosion will go on and on if we let it. I believe in calling a spade a spade and that is just what is going on here, so let us face it.
If you do not know where you are you will find out soon enough.

We will find out in time, Mr. Speaker. I will leave a few moments for the hon. Member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) but I do want to say this. The time is coming when, if we carry on the way we are, we will be as disorganized and confused as anybody could be. We must have something to rest our case on, some tradition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We have Canada.

We have Canada and Canadians, as I said before, but something more than that is involved. We do not have to yell on July 1st that this is Canada Day because everybody knows we are in Canada. But Dominion Day means more than just Canada as far as I am concerned. It represents more of a community together. I am not in favour of the bill before us.
Mr. Speaker, I too am opposed to the bill now before the House.
We are not surprised.

I am glad I do not surprise my republican friends across the way, and let me say I listened quietly and intently to what they said. But if in the wrath of a spoiled child who looks like he is not going to get a second helping of dessert the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) cannot contain himself I would ask him to leave the chamber, as I would be polite enough to do if the situation were reversed.
My objections to this legislation are these. First of all, a case for a change of name has not been made out. I for one, like most of my constituents in the north, am not prepared to pursue novelty for its own sake. We know that the unintelligent overthrowing of tradition and the pursuit of novelty for its own sake can lead only to anarchy.
Another reason I am opposed to this bill is that in my opinion it is another example of the spirit of tokenism that pervades the Government benches across the way. I see evidences of this all around me. No greater example of the spirit of tokenism has ever been given the country than the flag issue when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country, facing grave constitutional issues and

tremendous problems of unemployment and urban redevelopment, said to the people of Canada in effect; "Clothe your nakedness in a single maple leaf; if we give you this, all will be well".
Tokenism is something which I am prepared to fight everywhere I meet it, and I am prepared to fight it not only as a Canadian but more particularly as a northern Canadian. When I see what is occurring in this country and see a group of southern Canadians, not exclusively limited to the Government benches but pretty much grouped together over there, dedicated to tokens rather than real development, then I become frightened for those parts of the country which need real, serious and intelligent measures to improve the lot of the people.
I can guarantee one thing, that the token change envisaged in this legislation to change "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day" is the sort of thing I am not prepared to accept until a case has been made out. So far no one in speaking to this bill, including the mover and the seconder, have given me any reason why this change should be made at this time other than the fact that some Members, who as I have said are nicely grouped, feel that they could go back to their constituents and breathe more easily if they were able to bring about this change.
My third objection I can state in a sentence. If this is a good move, then the responsibility rests with the Government and a Minister of the Crown to introduce it, in which case it can be debated by the full House and exposed to the full glare of press and publicity. If the Prime Minister and the Members of his Cabinet choose to excite the daring and give new promise to the timid by changing the name of Dominion Day to Canada Day, then let them have the guts to bring in this change. But they are not going to sneak it in through the back door. May I call it six o'clock?
